round_scores.evidence: Opening request (no strong-smelling cooking) met with objections: Agent B: "A ban might be difficult... I can just close my door." Agent C: "Closing the door doesn't help the laundry in the service yard, though." Shows clear substantive disagreement about a ban and how to handle smells.

Agent D offers a procedural concession: "I can give a heads-up before I start cooking, so you can bring your clothes in?" Agent A responds that heads-up doesn't solve living-room smell: "That helps with the laundry, but it doesn't solve the smell in the living room. I work here." Conflict remains but participants are moving toward accommodations.

Agent C accepts heads-up: "Yeah, a heads-up would be great." Agent D proposes timing adjustment: "Agent A, what times do you usually work in the living room? I can try to cook when you're not there." Positions soften; disagreement persists but is being actively negotiated.
Agent A supplies scheduling information: "I'm usually on calls until about 7 p.m. on weekdays." (repeated). This reduces uncertainty but does not by itself settle the incompatibility.

Agent D proposes concrete timing: "Okay, so if I cook after 7 p.m. on weekdays, would that work?" Agent A accepts: "Yeah, after 7 works." Mutual, concrete spoken agreement resolving the core incompatibility about A's work-time and cooking smell.
Agent D summarizes the arrangement: "So, heads-up before I cook, and after 7 on weekdays. That works for everyone?" Agent B: "Yeah, that works for me." No substantive disagreement expressed.

substantive_insights: The initial demand for an outright ban was unrealistic given shared space and landlord constraints; practical scheduling was a workable alternative.
Two separate harm vectors mattered: laundry contamination (service yard) and direct intrusion into the living room during work calls; solutions needed to address both.
A combination of notification (heads-up) and time-based restriction resolved the incompatibility without requiring expense or landlord intervention.
